extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of experimental science, philosophers of science, and researchers evaluating inductive inference
extracted.subtask_description: Judging the strength of inductive/experimental inferences about causation using Mill-style Four Methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) and their combinations; includes practical requirements for experiments and natural 'experiments'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set of instances all exhibit the same effect and they share only one circumstance in common, that common circumstance is inferred to be the cause (or part of the cause) of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method identifies putative antecedents by finding the single circumstance common to multiple instances (example: 'dogs bark' — being a dog corresponds to barking). It does not by itself prove causation; it yields a candidate antecedent that requires further testing or corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare cases which are identical in all material respects except for the presence/absence of one antecedent; if the effect occurs only when that antecedent is present, attribute the effect to that antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires that the two cases be as alike as possible in all material circumstances save the one under test (A B C vs a b c). It is a direct method for proving causation, but demands careful control and repetition to exclude accidental differences (example: touching fire = burn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where degrees of an antecedent vary and the degree of the effect varies correspondingly, infer a causal connection between antecedent and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method uses proportional or correlated changes (concomitant variations) to infer dependence; exemplified by experiments where stronger galvanic charges produce proportionally shorter cadaveric rigidity. It supports causal inference by showing systematic correspondence of magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate and subtract the effects of all known causes from an observed phenomenon; the remaining 'residual' phenomenon points to unknown antecedents or new causes to be investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be a proper Residues application, effects of known causes should be calculated/estimated (ideally a priori) and subducted; residuals then motivate search for new causes (examples: comet period anomalies suggesting resisting medium; discovery of chemical elements in residues). If not calculated first, the example may instead illustrate Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method (Agreement + Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the Methods of Agreement and Difference to strengthen inductive claims: identify common antecedents across cases and then demonstrate via difference-type comparisons that varying that antecedent changes the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly valuable when causation of the aggregate antecedent is already established (e.g., death causes post-mortem changes); allows isolating which component of an aggregate antecedent (e.g., muscular irritability) is the operative cause by showing the consequence follows that component regardless of how it was produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural experiment / rapid single-change criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural occurrence that introduces one single, perfectly definite new circumstance and manifests the effect rapidly (so no other material change can intervene) satisfies the Method of Difference and can serve as proof of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when clouds withdraw briefly and dew deposition begins immediately; such cases permit attribution of the effect to the single changed circumstance (clear sky causing increased radiative cooling). Use these as strong corroboration when they meet the rapidity/singleness condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeatability and scale-extrapolation of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments should demonstrate the effect reproducibly on manageable (often small) scales and provide reason to conclude the same operation at nature's larger scale will produce the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small-scale cooling experiments that show dew formation at a certain temperature justify extrapolation to natural settings when the same physical mechanism is present; repeat experiments sufficiently often to exclude accidental results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for confounders / ensuring comparable cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When using Difference or Agreement methods, ensure cases compared are alike in all other material respects so that the attributed antecedent is not confounded by accidental differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps include comparing paired parts of the same subject (e.g., left/right limbs of the same animal) and repeating across many subjects to exclude pathological or accidental differences; failure to secure comparability weakens inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate independence from causes of antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that an effect depends on a particular antecedent rather than on other effects that accompany it, demonstrate the same effect whenever that antecedent is present regardless of how the antecedent was produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., show that late cadaveric rigidity follows high muscular irritability whether the irritability arises from paralysis, cold, or good nutrition; this rules out alternative explanations tied to particular causes of the antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality principle in concomitant variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Causal inference is strengthened when varying the antecedent in degree produces corresponding, often roughly proportional, changes in the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a range of intensities (e.g., galvanic charges) and show monotonic/regular change in the effect (shorter rigidity with stronger charge) to support a causal, quantitative relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate and account for known causes before invoking new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Before ascribing an observed discrepancy to a novel cause, quantitatively estimate the effects of known causes and subtract them to reveal any genuine residual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in astronomy and acoustics: compute expected contributions (e.g., from gravitation, precession, heat effects) and only then treat the remainder as evidence of a new phenomenon or cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: Agreement alone cannot prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement by itself is insufficient to establish causal relations; it can produce candidate antecedents but needs corroboration by other methods or further testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Agreement outputs as hypotheses to be tested by Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues, or controlled experiments; beware of spurious commonalities that are not causal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of decomposing phenomena into A, B, C elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical limitation of the Four Methods is that they presuppose the reduction of complex phenomena into distinct antecedent elements (A, B, C...), which is often the hardest step in investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that identifying the relevant antecedent elements is non-trivial and may require insight, hypothesis, and iterative analysis; the methods provide tests for candidate decompositions but do not always show how to obtain them initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of deduction and hypothesis alongside induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction and the construction of hypotheses often play a necessary role in complex inquiries; the Four Methods primarily supply tests of induction (proof), complementing hypothesis-driven discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deduction to frame hypotheses but employ the Four Methods to test and prove them against observation and experiment; historical scientific discoveries often required both deduction and the experimental methods described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple independent lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive assurance of causation is strongest when diverse methods and independent types of evidence (agreement, difference, concomitant variation, residues, natural experiments) converge on the same conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect different forms of corroboration (laboratory experiments, natural experiments, quantitative concomitant variation, residual anomalies) to achieve high confidence, as in the dew example or Brown-Séquard's physiological investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical test for inductive claims (analogy to syllogistic test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive claims should be judged by conformity to explicit rules or models (the Four Methods) much as deductive arguments are judged by syllogistic form; adherence to these tests renders inductive inferences more conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Four Methods as a checklist to evaluate whether an inductive argument truly establishes causation rather than relying solely on empirical correspondence or intuitive fit; this is the aim of inductive logic—providing standards of proof.
